title: If My Phone Distracts Me… Except There Is No If
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Reviewing his students' WOOP goal-setting worksheets, Dave Stuart Jr. notices a recurring pattern: students identify their phones as an Obstacle to their goals and then write an if/then plan of 'If I get distracted by my phone, then I will put it away' — a plan he uses as the springboard for a live classroom Woodenization moment. He walks students through why the 'if' framing is flawed, laying out two scenarios where a phone sits nearby during goal-striving work: either the student resists it (which drains finite concentration and makes the work less enjoyable even though it gets done) or the student doesn't resist it (and the work doesn't get done at all). Both outcomes, he argues, are worse than removing the temptation altogether. He physically demonstrates his proposed solution during class — placing his phone outside the door and shutting it — modeling the exact behavior he wants students to adopt: separate the phone from the goal-striving environment entirely rather than relying on willpower to resist it in the moment. He closes candidly acknowledging that not every student will act on the advice, but frames the three-minute lesson as worthwhile regardless.
points: Spotting the same flawed 'if/then' pattern across multiple students' WOOP worksheets ('If I get distracted by my phone, then I will put it away') turns individual student writing into the occasion for a whole-class teaching moment.

Reframing 'there is no if' collapses the illusion of willpower-based phone management: with a phone present, a goal-striving session either fails outright or succeeds at a hidden cost to concentration and enjoyment.
Physically walking to the door and setting his own phone outside mid-lesson lets Stuart Woodenize the behavior he's teaching rather than merely describing it.

Naming the phone's pull honestly ('always going to be more immediately engaging and entertaining and rewarding') avoids moralizing and instead treats phone distraction as a predictable, structural problem with a structural fix.
Stuart's closing acknowledgment that not all students will act on the advice models realistic expectations for behavior-change teaching without undercutting the value of delivering the lesson.
quotes: Yeah — when it comes to phones distracting us, there is no IF.
Even though you've completed the goal-striving behavior, it required much more effort (and was likely much less enjoyable) than it would have been had you put the phone in a different room.

is to take your phone, put it in another room, and close the door. Put in the amount of time you have planned for your goal-striving activity, then get up, go to the other room, and do what you'd like on your phone.
Are all of my students going to take heed of this advice? No. But are some? Yes. Three minutes well spent, then.
What I'm trying to do here is Woodenize how to create a more success-oriented environment for goal-striving behaviors. It really starts as simply as chucking the phone out the door.
